content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).
I'll gather the diff under review, then launch 4 parallel cleanup agents.

input.prompt:
You are reviewing a code change for the EFFICIENCY angle only. Do NOT hunt for correctness bugs.

The change adds a compact transcript (`transcript.jsonl`) to committed checkpoints in the Entire CLI. The diff under review is at `/tmp/simplify-diff.txt` — read it. Primary changed file is `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/committed.go` (functions `writeTranscript`, `writeCompactTranscript`, `compactAgentName`, `replaceTranscript`). Background: `codex.SanitizePortableTranscript` (in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/codex/transcript.go`) and `transcriptcompact.Compact` (in `cmd/entire/cli/transcript/compact/`) both fully parse/re-marshal the entire transcript — they are EXPENSIVE passes. A key design goal of this change was that sanitization runs at most once per write path (not double-sanitizing already-sanitized bytes).

Your task: flag wasted work the diff introduces — redundant computation or repeated parsing/marshaling of the transcript, work that runs twice across `writeTranscript` (initial write) and `replaceTranscript` (finalize), unnecessary byte copies, or expensive work on hot paths. Verify the "sanitize at most once per path" goal actually holds in both paths. Also check whether `compactAgentName` does repeated lookups that could be hoisted.

Be concrete: confirm whether `writeCompactTranscript` re-sanitizes bytes that the initial-write path already sanitized (it should NOT), and whether the compact generation duplicates parsing already done for chunking.

input.prompt:
You are reviewing a code change for the ALTITUDE angle only. Do NOT hunt for correctness bugs.

The change adds a compact transcript (`transcript.jsonl`) to committed checkpoints in the Entire CLI. The diff under review is at `/tmp/simplify-diff.txt` — read it. Primary changed file is `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/committed.go` (functions `writeTranscript`, `writeCompactTranscript`, `compactAgentName`, `replaceTranscript`). Your task: check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered onto shared infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding agent-specific special cases.

Focus on:
- The Codex-specific sanitization is now coded inline in TWO places: `writeTranscript` (`if opts.Agent == agent.AgentTypeCodex { transcriptBytes = codex.SanitizePortableTranscript(transcriptBytes) }`) and `replaceTranscript` (the `compactBytes` block). Is per-agent transcript sanitization the kind of thing that should live behind a shared seam (e.g. an agent-type-dispatched "prepare transcript bytes for storage" step) rather than two inline `if agentType == Codex` checks in the checkpoint store? Is there already an agent-dispatch mechanism (look in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/`) where this normalization belongs?

Be pragmatic: only flag altitude issues where generalizing is clearly warranted by the current code (two call sites of the same special case is a signal). Note when the inline approach is acceptably scoped.

Return a concise list of findings: `file:line`, one-line summary, why the current depth is fragile, and the deeper mechanism to prefer (naming the existing seam if one exists). If altitude is fine, say so explicitly. Do not propose changes for other angles.

content.text:
All four agents have reported. Let me dedup and decide.

- **Reuse:** nothing actionable — `compactAgentName`, the test helpers, and the sanitize block are not duplicating existing helpers.
- **Simplification:** none — guards, comments, and tests judged already minimal.
- **Efficiency:** none — confirmed "sanitize once per path" holds; no double-sanitization or wasted parsing.
- **Altitude:** one finding — the `if agentType == AgentTypeCodex { SanitizePortableTranscript }` appears in two places; proposes a new `TranscriptNormalizer` agent interface.

The altitude finding is the only candidate, and I'm **skipping** it. Reasoning:

1. **Scope:** the fix requires a new interface in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/agent.go` plus a codex-agent implementation — well outside the reviewed diff. The `/simplify` rules say to skip fixes that require changes well outside the diff.
2. **One site is pre-existing:** the `writeTranscript` Codex block came from main; only the `replaceTranscript` block is mine. Generalizing would refactor unrelated existing code and widen the agent package's public surface — an architectural decision, not a cleanup.
3. **The two sites aren't actually the same operation.** In `writeTranscript`, sanitized bytes feed the full.jsonl chunks, content hash, *and* compact. In `replaceTranscript`, sanitization deliberately scopes to the compact only (chunks/hash stay raw — the intended boundary from this PR). A shared "normalize for storage" helper would *obscure* that deliberate difference. This is why the reuse and simplification agents both judged the inline form acceptable.

Let me clean up.

Here's what I found.

## The file is new to this PR, and it tests a different layer

- `committed_compact_transcript_test.go` was **added by this PR** (commit `afd94281e`); it does not exist on `origin/main` (`git diff` shows status `A`).
- The "existing compact-transcript tests" are in **`cmd/entire/cli/transcript/compact/*_test.go`** (`compact_test.go`, `codex_test.go`, etc.). Those test the **`Compact()` transformation in isolation** — given raw agent JSONL, does it produce the right compact format.
- This new file tests the **checkpoint-store integration** — that `GitStore.WriteCommitted`/`UpdateCommitted` actually generate `transcript.jsonl`, write it into the branch tree, scope it to the checkpoint start, set the metadata pointer to `full.jsonl`, and regenerate/sanitize on finalize. That behavior is exactly what this PR introduces, and **nothing on `main` covered it** (`checkpoint_test.go`'s only `transcript.jsonl` hits are the unrelated on-disk `agent-transcript.jsonl`).

So the file belongs here — it's the unit coverage for the new store-layer code. It's complementary to, not a duplicate of, the compact-package tests.

## But you're partly right — some assertions over-reach

One test re-validates the **compact format**, which is the compact package's job, not the store's. In `TestWriteCommitted_WritesCompactTranscript`:

```go
for i, line := range lines {
    if line.V != 1 { ... }                       // compact-format detail
    if line.Agent != "claude-code" { ... }       // compact-format detail
}
if lines[0].Type != "user" || lines[1].Type != "assistant" { ... }  // compact-format detail
```

The `v`, `agent`, and per-line `type` shape are already asserted in `transcript/compact/codex_test.go` etc. The store test only needs to prove it *wrote and scoped the file* (exists in tree, non-empty, pointer correct, scoped content present) — which the other tests already do. This matches your own guidance ([[feedback_test_scope_to_unit.md]]: don't re-test a dependency's output from a consumer's tests).

The store-specific behavior in the file (writes into tree, scoping by start line, pointer = `full.jsonl`, non-compactable fallback, finalize regen, Codex sanitize-on-finalize) is *not* redundant and should stay.

Want me to trim the format-level assertions down to the store-layer ones? That'd tighten the file to its actual unit without losing real coverage.
